## Results

The STAP process consists of two sequential steps: controlled shrinkage and conformal transfer. First, a silicone substrate (Ecoflex film) is omnidirectional pre-strained to a defined ratio and secured on an acrylic frame to maintain tension (Supplementary Fig. 1, Movie 1). EGaIn circuits are then screen-printed onto the stretched silicone substrate. Upon releasing the tension, the substrate contracts, resulting in a uniform reduction in the circuit size and forming microcircuits (Fig. 1a). Subsequently, the microcircuits are transferred conformally onto the target fiber using a water-soluble PVA carrier film. After dissolving the PVA layer, the EGaIn microcircuits remain intact and adherent to the fiber surface (Supplementary Movie 2). To demonstrate functional applicability, we spray-coated an EL layer consisting of ZnS:Cu particles dispersed in a styrene-ethylene-butylene-styrene (SEBS) matrix onto the fiber, achieving a light-emitting array with individually addressable pixels (Fig. 1b).

The shrinkage ratio of EGaIn microcircuits can be precisely controlled (Supplementary Fig. 2), enabling up to an 80% reduction in circuit area relative to the original printed design while preserving structural integrity and pattern fidelity (Fig. 1c). These microcircuits can be fabricated at arbitrary position along meter-length continuous fiber (Fig. 1d) and achieve 360° full circumferential coverage, thereby maximizing the available surface area for functional device integration (Fig. 1e). The transfer process preserves the microcircuit patterns without noticeable distortion. Owing to the ultrathin nature of the PVA carrier film (20 μm), residual PVA on the fiber surface is negligible and does not compromise the overall flexibility of the system.

The EL functionality of the pixels is driven by the high electric field generated within the microcircuits under pulsed voltage excitation. When an alternating electric field exceeding 2 kV/mm is applied across the luminescent layer coated on the circuits, electrons in ZnS:Cu absorb energy, being promoted to excited states, and emit photons upon returning to their ground states26. Controllable light emission is achieved by optimizing the interelectrode spacing within the microcircuits to maintain an electric field sufficient for luminescence while avoiding dielectric breakdown (Fig. 1f). The STAP strategy improves processing resolution through controlled size reduction, while the circuit fabrication itself remains a macroscale process. This approach readily produces electrode gaps as narrow as 35 μm (Supplementary Fig. 3), exceeding the typical resolution limit of conventional screen-printing methods (50 μm), which is constrained by the mesh size.

Screen-printable conductive ink is crucial for fabricating EGaIn microcircuits. We developed a water-based EGaIn/sericin ink composed of EGaIn with a melting point of 16 °C as the conductive component and silk sericin as the stabilizer (Fig. 2a). Bulk EGaIn was dispersed into EGaIn microparticles (EMPs) by blending it at 20,000 rpm. The resulting EMPs were slightly oxidized in water, forming a surface oxide layer that improves their affinity with sericin. Sericin contains amino acids such as serine, tyrosine, and aspartic acid, which have oxygen-rich functional side groups, as well as cysteine with sulfur-containing side groups27. Consequently, sericin can stably adhere to the surface of EMPs through hydrogen bonding and coordination interactions. This adsorption creates a physical barrier between individual EMPs. Furthermore, sericin is negatively charged in neutral aqueous solution (isoelectric point = 4)28, inducing electrostatic repulsion among sericin-coated EMPs due to Coulombic forces (Fig. 2b). The combined steric and electrostatic stabilization effects allow the EMPs to remain well-dispersed in water for more than one week without agglomeration (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 5).

Microscopic and spectroscopic characterizations confirm the interactions between EMPs and sericin. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) coupled with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) reveals a homogeneous distribution of O, N, and S elements across the EMP surfaces, confirming the presence of sericin adhesion (Fig. 2d). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images directly show a continuous shell layer of sericin coating the EMPs (Fig. 2e). Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) exhibits a red shift of 12.5 cm−1 in the characteristic sericin absorption peak at 3267.3 cm−1 after adsorption onto EMPs (Fig. 2f), suggesting hydrogen bonding formation between sericin and the surface oxide layer29,30. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) further reveals the interactions between sulfur atoms in cysteine residues and the EMP surface. The S 2p spectrum exhibit two characteristic peaks at 167.3 eV and 168.4 eV (Fig. 2g), corresponding to free thiol groups in cysteine31. Upon binding with EMPs, these peaks shift to lower binding energies (160.6 eV and 163.0 eV), consistent with the formation of metal-sulfur bonds or coordination32,33. The peak at 158.8 eV is attributed to the overlap of Ga 3s34. This distinct shift of S 2p peaks provides strong evidence of chemical interactions. Complementary N 1s spectra (Supplementary Fig. 4) reflect changes in nitrogen coordination environments, offering additional support for the sericin-mediated stabilization mechanism.

The affinity between EMPs and sericin endow the EGaIn/sericin ink with high colloidal stability and excellent printability. The size of EMPs can be tuned by varying the blending duration, yielding particles with an averaged diameter of approximately 3 μm that is suitable for unobstructed passage through screen meshes (Fig. 2h, Supplementary Fig. 6). Zeta potential measurements reveal a more negative surface charge for the EGaIn/sericin composite (−12.4 mV) compared to pure sericin solution (−7.4 mV) (Fig. 2i), suggesting that EMPs promote ionization of acidic functional groups in sericin, thereby enhancing electrostatic stabilization. Rheological analyses show that the incorporation of EMPs increases the viscosity of the sericin matrix, consistent with strong interfacial interactions. Notably, the EGaIn/sericin system exhibits a pronounced shear-thinning behavior (Fig. 2j), which is an essential requirement for high-resolution screen printing, as it facilitates flow during printing while ensuring shape retention thereafter35.

The printed circuit patterns are initially non-conductive due to the presence of surface oxides and surrounding polymer barriers, which typically require additional sintering steps, such as mechanical compression or chemical treatment, to form conductive pathways in conventional EGaIn circuits36. Remarkably, the STAP strategy integrates two in situ sintering mechanisms without requiring external interventions. The first mechanism, shrinkage-induced sintering, occurs autonomously during substrate contraction. Prior to screen printing, a pre-stretched silicone substrate is partially treated with air plasma (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Figs. 7, 8) to enhance ink adhesion. A plasma treatment duration of 3 min enables robust attachment of the printed circuit patterns (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Movie 3). Subsequent release of the pre-strain triggers spontaneous conductivity development (Fig. 3c). In samples with pre-stretch ratios of 450%, 300%, and 150%, the resistance evolution follows a characteristic three-stage profile: starting from infinity, dropping rapidly to a finite value, and finally stabilizing (Fig. 3e). All groups reached a resistance of 102 Ω after an initial 50% strain release, exhibiting diminishing returns with further release. Higher pre-strain ratios resulted in lower final resistances (Fig. 3f), indicating more efficient sintering of the EMPs. Mechanistic analysis suggests that the shrinkage of the substrate reduces the interparticle spacing until the friction force (Ff) between EMPs and the substrate exceeds the mechanical strength of the particle shells (Fig. 3d), resulting in shell rupture and EGaIn fusion. Larger pre-stretch amplifies this compressive force, thereby enhancing electrical conductivity. Notably, this sintering process preserves pattern integrity despite internal particle rearrangement.

The transfer-sintering mechanism is activated during the transfer of shrunken EGaIn microcircuits from the silicone substrates to PVA films. As the PVA is peeled from the silicone, continuous metallic patterns become visible on the PVA surface (Fig. 3g), confirming the formation of a conductive pathway. In situ SEM characterization reveals that EGaIn adheres to both surfaces without detectable EMP residues (Fig. 3h), indicating complete sintering. This transfer-induced sintering arises from competitive interfacial adhesion: the plasma-activated silicone and the PVA film both exhibit strong affinity to the EMPs, showing adhesion forces of 0.53 μN and 0.79 μN, respectively (Supplementary Figs. 11, 12). Consequently, the separation process ruptures the oxide shells, triggering instantaneous liquid metal coalescence. The stronger affinity between PVA and EMPs results in preferential transfer of the EGaIn circuits to the PVA surface. The affinity of PVA is primarily attributed to hydrogen bonds between the hydroxyl groups of PVA and the EMPs. To verify the role of hydroxyl groups, comparative adhesion tests were conducted using polyvinyl butyral (PVB), a polymer structurally analogous to PVA but with a portion of its hydroxyl groups blocked by acetal formation. Mechanical measurements reveal that the adhesion force of PVB films toward EMPs is 0.46 μN, significantly lower than that of PVA (0.79 μN) (Supplementary Fig. 12e, f). Laser confocal microscopy further reveals the morphological evolution and gap narrowing during dual-stage sintering, confirming that the STAP strategy synergistically combines circuit miniaturization and conductivity restoration without compromising structural integrity (Fig. 3i, Supplementary Fig. 13). Furthermore, the reduced feature sizes in EGaIn microcircuits directly enhance device integration density, an outcome governed by two principal parameters: the original screen mesh specifications and the applied shrinkage ratio.

The ultimate resolution achievable by STAP is governed by the initial screen-printing precision and the shrinkage behavior of the EMPs on the silicone platform. The intrinsic resolution (Ff) is defined by the screen-printing process determines the fineness of the microcircuit patterns. Screens with higher mesh counts provide finer patterning but reduce ink passage, lowering the amount of deposited EGaIn and creating a fundamental compromise between resolution and conductivity. In this work, 300-mesh represents a practical upper limit. Finer meshes fail to transfer sufficient ink to form continuous pathways even after shrinkage. As shown in Fig. 3j, the x-axis represents the pre-stretch ratio, which correlates with the magnitude of Ff that drives sintering. The y-axis denotes the EMP surface coverage, where lower values impede electrical percolation. The phase boundary identifies the combinations of pre-stretch and coverage that maintain conductivity above the percolation threshold. Moving along this boundary toward higher Ff enables smaller feature sizes while preserving electrical continuity (see Table S2 for electrical conductivity for each point). The resolution and lateral deviation of microcircuits fabricated with different screen meshes were systematically examined under an extreme area shrinkage of 80% (Table S1). This parametric framework study addresses the multi-parameter optimization challenge and facilitates the fabrication of high-resolution microcircuits (Fig. 3k). During shrinking, the compressive stress originating from the recovery of the silicone is transmitted upward through the microcircuit (Supplementary Fig. 14). Under extreme shrinkage, this stress can induce overflow of EMPs beyond the designed pattern boundaries. Since further improvement in the as-printed resolution is hindered by insufficient ink transfer through higher-mesh screens, these two factors together limit the final attainable result resolution (Supplementary Fig. 15).

The capillary-driven transfer process enables precise conformal wrapping of EGaIn microcircuit onto fiber substrates. Aramid fiber is chosen as the substrate due to its intrinsic hydrophilicity and relatively high dielectric constant. When a water droplet is introduced at the interface between the PVA film and the fiber, capillary forces induce radial liquid propagation along both the axial and circumferential directions of the fiber, simultaneously dissolving the PVA matrix and promoting interfacial adhesion (Fig. 4a). This process is governed by the thermodynamics of wetting, as described by the following equation (w = water, F = fiber, P = PVA):

ΔG T,p = γ w,P + γ w,F − γ Air,P − γ Air,F (1)

Spontaneous wrapping occurs when ΔG T,p < 0. Given the hydrophilic nature of both PVA and aramid fibers (contact angles < 90°), the following relationships hold:

cosθ w,P = (γ Air,P − γ w,P) / γ w,Air > 0 (2)

cosθ w,F = (γ Air,F − γ w,F) / γ w,Air > 0 (3)

Substituting (2) and (3) into Eq. (1) confirms ΔG T,p < 0, validating the self-driven nature of the transfer mechanism. This ensures conformal contact and reliable adhesion of the microcircuit to the fiber surface without external energy input.

Consequently, water droplets undergo spontaneous downward propagation through the capillary channels formed between the fiber and PVA film. Hydration-induced plasticization softens the PVA, reducing its modulus from 5 GPa to a compliant, rubbery state that enables conformal wrapping around the fiber circumference. Meanwhile, the decreased interfacial tension γ w,P further promotes wetting and adhesion (Fig. 4b). This transfer process demonstrates broad applicability across varying degrees of dimensional reduction (2D→1D). EGaIn microcircuits with shrinkage ratios ranging from 50% to 80% retain structural integrity and pattern fidelity after transfer (Fig. 4c), enabling on-demand fabrication of fiber devices with tunable feature sizes down to 60 μm (Fig. 4d).

Preserving pattern fidelity during fiber device integration is critical, where any circuit discontinuities or short circuits would lead to device failure. Radial gap analysis reveals a dimensional variation of ≤5% across the full 360° circumference (Fig. 4e), confirming the non-destructive nature of our transfer process. Notably, this transfer step can also be applied to fibers of different materials and diameters (Supplementary Fig. 19), and can be repeated on one fiber to construct a multilayer circuit (Supplementary Fig. 20).

The resulting fiber devices exhibit exceptional mechanical compliance, enduring 16,000 bending cycles at a curvature radius of 1.6 cm with only a 1.4% increase in resistance. The fiber microcircuit can be bent to a critical radius (rc, defined as the bending radius at which ΔR/R₀ begins to exceed 200%) of 2.3 mm (Fig. 4f), demonstrating good robustness for wearable applications. This performance originates from the intrinsic fluidity and strain-insensitive conductivity of EGaIn, as confirmed by microscopy observations of continuous EGaIn pathways during bending (Supplementary Fig. 21). The bending limit of the fiber microcircuit is governed by the PVA adhesive layer, whose flexibility increases with temperature and humidity, leading to different critical radii across different environmental conditions (Supplementary Fig. 22). The shrinkage ratio of EGaIn microcircuits, modulated via the STAP process, directly governs the performance of fiber devices. Capacitance measurements of interdigitated electrodes reveal a 103 enhancement (10 Hz) as the shrinkage ratio increases from 50% to 80% (Fig. 4g), attributed to a reduced interelectrode spacing and increased effective electrode area.

The EL performance of the pixels is determined by electric field intensity (E), which we optimized through precise control of the shrinkage ratio. Finite element simulations of the electric field distribution (Fig. 4h) identified 2 kV/mm as the minimum field required to activate ZnS:Cu particles. Excessively large gaps (>50 μm) result in a reduced number of activated phosphor particles due to field decay, whereas undersized gaps (<25 μm) lead to highly concentrated fields that induce dielectric breakdown. Although the aramid fiber substrate has high tolerance to strong electric fields37, the breakdown of the emissive functional layer remains affecting luminescence efficiency. Thus, an intermediate gap width is required to achieve optimal luminescence. Experimentally, peak luminance is achieved at gap distances of 50–60 μm, where the simulated electric field maximizes the excitation area within the phosphor layer while avoiding dielectric failure (Fig. 4i).

Guided by these design principles, we successfully fabricated an EL pixel array on a fiber. The intrinsic flexibility of the fiber, the EGaIn circuitry, and the SEBS matrix works synergistically to sustain device functionality under mechanical deformation, as demonstrated by a fully operational curved array (Fig. 4j). The pixel array is designed with (2n-3) contact points to individually address n EL pixels, maximizing the number of controllable elements within a limited area (5 contacts controlling 7 pixels in Fig. 4k). Functionalization was carried out by spray-coating a ZnS:Cu/SEBS dispersion, followed by ambient drying to form the electroluminescence layer. Selective pixel activation can be achieved by electrical addressing through designated contacts (Fig. 4l, Supplementary Movie 4), enabling the multiplexed display on a single fiber. Luminance stability remains 94% when bent to a radius of 15 mm, but then decreases rapidly as the curvature increases further (Supplementary Fig. 23). Single-fiber displays, featuring pixel-level addressability, can be seamlessly woven into protective garments for dynamic visual communication. In critical scenarios such as firefighting, rescue operations, and outdoor exploration, they can provide real-time navigation, hazard alerts, or team status. They also enable monitoring of vital signs for medical assistance and facilitate communication by displaying information for individuals with speech or language barriers. It is noted that the STAP process is also compatible with other typical commercially available inks besides the EGaIn/sericin ink (Supplementary Fig. 24). This STAP strategy overcomes the long-standing challenge of integrating high-precision microcircuits onto curved fiber substrates, paving the way for multifunctional and high-density wearable electronics. Further efforts on developing automated stretching and continuous transfer systems could improve the scalability of STAP and facilitate its adoption in practical manufacturing settings.

## Methods

Materials
All materials were used as received. EGaIn (75%Ga, 25%In, melting point 16 °C) was purchased from Alibaba. Silk sericin and PVA (MW: 100,000) were purchased from Macklin. ZnS:Cu phosphor powder was purchased from Shanghai Keyan Phosphor Technology Co., Ltd. Ecoflex 0030 was purchased from Smooth-On. Aramid fiber was purchased from DuPont. SEBS and chloroform were purchased from Sigma. Ag/AgCl ink and PEDOT:PSS ink were purchased from Prtronic, and the carbon ink was obtained from Loctite. All inks were used as received, without further purification or modification.

Fabrication of EGaIn/sericin ink
First, prepare 100 ml of 2 wt% sericin aqueous solution. Using a syringe, inject 4 ml of EGaIn into the solution, and disperse it using an IKA mill at a speed of 20,000 rpm for 1 min. Subsequently, cool the mixture to 20 °C using an ice-water bath, and repeat the process three times.

Fabrication of Shrunk microcircuits
The fabrication of shrunk microcircuits was carried out in two main steps: screen printing and pattern shrinkage. First, a 200 μm-thick Ecoflex film was omnidirectionally stretched and mounted onto a clean acrylic frame under tension. Next, a patterned screen was placed on the surface of the Ecoflex film as a mask, and the sample was exposed to air plasma for 3 min. Then, EGaIn/sericin ink was screen-printed onto the film. After drying, the EGaIn circuit was formed on the silicone substrate. Pattern shrinkage was achieved by releasing the pre-strained Ecoflex film from the acrylic frame, resulting in the contraction of the substrate and the formation of the final shrunk microcircuits. All the processes, including the fabrication of shrunk microcircuits and their transfer, were performed at 20 °C and 50% relative humidity, unless otherwise specified.

Process of transferring microcircuits
The transfer of the microcircuit was accomplished using a PVA carrier film. A 20 μm thick PVA film was prepared by casting, then handled with tweezers, and its bottom surface was briefly contacted with a water surface for 0.5 s to achieve partial hydration. The moistened film was then carefully laminated onto the Ecoflex substrate bearing the microcircuit. After allowing the PVA film to partially dissolve, the assembly was dried under 60 °C for 30 min to enhance adhesion and facilitate the formation of a continuous bilayer. Finally, the PVA film was peeled off, transferring the highly conductive, intact EGaIn microcircuit to the PVA surface.

Fabrication of single-point controllable EL fiber device
The fabricated PVA film carrying the microcircuit was placed onto the target fiber surface. Using a syringe, water was carefully applied along the edges of the PVA film to allow capillary action to penetrate the interface, enabling the circuit to adhere to the fiber surface and forming the fiber circuit. Special care should be taken to ensure that the water is applied to the gaps between the PVA film and the fiber, rather than directly on the surface of the PVA film. Upon complete dissolution of the PVA, the circuit remained attached to the fiber, forming a continuous fiber-integrated microcircuit. The assembly was then dried at 60 °C for 30 min to enhance stability. Subsequently, an electroluminescent layer was applied by spray-coating a formulated ink suspension consisting of ZnS:Cu fluorescent powder, SEBS elastomer, and chloroform (mass ratio: 1 g: 0.5 g: 5 g). The coated fiber was dried again to evaporate the solvent, forming a solid emissive composite layer. Finally, the device was completed by connecting the fiber circuit to an external power supply for activation and operation.

Morphology characterization
Transmission electron microscopy (JEOL, JEM-2100F) and scanning electron microscopy (Thermo Fisher, Phenom XL G2 Desktop SEM) were used to characterize the morphology of EGaIn microparticles and microcircuits. The in situ observation of PVA/Ecoflex delamination and the shrinkage-sintering of microcircuits was carried out using an SEM equipped with an in situ tensile holder. Image processing and EGaIn microparticle diameter analysis were conducted using ImageJ software. Laser confocal microscopy (Zeiss, LSM900) was used to observe surface morphology changes during the shrinking and transfer processes of the microcircuits.

Spectroscopic and rheological characterization
Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, BRUKER, VERTEX) was used to evaluate hydrogen bonding interactions between EGaIn and sericin. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Fisher, ESCALAB Xi+) was used to analyze the coordination interactions between EGaIn and sericin. Viscosity measurements were conducted using a rotational rheometer (Anton Paar, MCR302).

Electrical and mechanical characterization
Electrical characterization was performed using an electrochemical workstation (Shanghai Chenhua, CHI760E). Mechanical tests were conducted using a SHIMADZU AGS-X universal testing machine. For simultaneous electromechanical characterization, the fiber device was mounted onto the tensile tester while electrically connected to the workstation via wires. Data acquisition from both instruments was synchronized through time alignment to correlate mechanical strain with electrical response. Repeated bending deformation was performed at a maximum curvature radius of 16 mm, at 20 °C and relative humidity of 50%, with a frequency of 1 Hz. The samples were stored in a temperature- and humidity-controlled chamber for 3 h before the test.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents a highly original approach to addressing the persistent challenge of integrating microscale circuits onto curved fiber surfaces. The proposed shrinkage-transfer-assisted printing (STAP) method elegantly bridges the gap between 2D circuit fabrication and 1D fiber device realization, achieving impressive miniaturization (up to 80% shrinkage) and 360° conformal coverage. The concept is novel, technically sound, and well supported by systematic experiments. The combination of stress-engineered silicone substrates, EGaIn/sericin ink chemistry, and capillary-driven transfer represents a meaningful advance in fiber-based electronics.
The manuscript is generally well written, visually clear, and methodologically detailed. It convincingly demonstrates functionality through the electroluminescent fiber device. The work is clearly distinct from previously published studies—including our earlier Nature Communications paper on integrated microfibre electronics—by offering a different dimensional transformation and processing strategy.
That said, a few aspects need clarification and strengthening before acceptance. These concern (1) the universality and scalability of the claimed “universal fabrication strategy,” (2) quantitative treatment of the scaling-down limit for metallic patterns, and (3) mechanical durability and interfacial reliability under extended cyclic deformation.
Overall, this is an excellent and innovative contribution that will attract broad attention in the field of fiber electronics and soft-matter circuit integration. The concept of geometric transformation from 2D to 1D is elegant, and the results are compelling.
Addressing the issues above, particularly regarding the scaling limit and mechanical reliability, will further strengthen the manuscript’s impact and technical completeness.
Major Comments
- The Introduction concludes that STAP is a “universal fabrication strategy,” yet experimental demonstrations are limited to EGaIn and PVA-based transfer. To substantiate this claim, the authors should briefly discuss whether the STAP process is compatible with other inks (e.g., silver nanoparticle, conductive polymer) or elastomeric substrates.
- A comparative comment on scalability with respect to textile-level or roll-to-roll fabrication methods would provide valuable context for its practical universality.
- What is possible resolution and Scaling-Down Limitations?
- While the manuscript demonstrates a 60 μm feature size and 35 μm electrode gaps, it remains unclear what factors fundamentally limit further miniaturization, whether by the screen mesh resolution, ink rheology, or mechanical shrinkage threshold of the substrate. Please provide indetail.
- Providing a scaling analysis or discussing the potential challenges in pushing esolution below 50 μm would be insightful. For instance, could oxide shell rupture or uneven compressive stress during shrinkage impose a lower limit?
- The manuscript claims retention of 98.6 % conductivity after 16,000 bending cycles, which is impressive. However, the detailed stress conditions (bending radius, strain amplitude, test frequency) should be more explicitly stated in Methods or figure captions to allow fair comparison with prior works.
- Since the circuit–fiber interface is critical, it would be helpful to discuss or test failure modes such as delamination or crack initiation, particularly under humidity or temperature variation. Supplementary Fig. 14 shows morphological stability but does not provide long-term cycling data.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript is generally well written and clearly presented. However, there are several issues that limit the overall scope and relevence of the work.
Material specificity:
The materials used in the study are very specialized and are not easily replaced or adapted to other functional materials (substrate, ink, GaIn ....)
Scalability and reproducibility:
Key steps in the process—such as pre-stretching, tension release, transferring onto a PVA sheet, water-assisted transfer, and the shrinkage of the printed circuits—introduce a lot of variability and are not easily scalable. As a result, achieving consistent reproducibility is challenging. In addition, the conductivity variations that come from shrinkage sintering and transfer sintering need to be supported with more detailed statistical data.
Multilayer printing limitations:
The approach does not seem capable of true multilayer printing. In the demonstrated device, the conductive layer is printed and transferred onto the thread, while the luminescent layer is applied by coating rather than printing. This highlights an inherent limitation of the technique.
Limited use on small-diameter substrates:
The method is demonstrated only on threads a few millimeters in diameter. Its potential for use on finer fibers or true one-dimensional substrates is not addressed, which restricts the broader relevance of the work.

Summary Comment:
This manuscript presents a highly original approach to addressing the persistent challenge of integrating microscale circuits onto curved fiber surfaces. The proposed shrinkage-transfer-assisted printing (STAP) method elegantly bridges the gap between 2D circuit fabrication and 1D fiber device realization, achieving impressive miniaturization (up to 80% shrinkage) and 360° conformal coverage. The concept is novel, technically sound, and well supported by systematic experiments. The combination of stress-engineered silicone substrates, EGaIn/sericin ink chemistry, and capillary-driven transfer represents a meaningful advance in fiber-based electronics.

Reply:
We appreciate the insightful questions regarding resolution and scaling-down limitations. Since Comments #3-5 are closely related, we address them collectively below. We have supplemented the discussion with schematic illustrations, SEM characterizations and additional data. The fundamental limits on resolution and miniaturization arise from two main aspects:
(i) Printing resolution on the pre-stretched silicone substrate. The initial patterning fidelity is governed by the screen-printing process. The resolution here refers to the clarity and continuity of the printed EGaIn/sericin pattern after the ink passes through the screen mesh. This printed pattern must be optically distinguishable and electrically continuous after shrinkage. Screen mesh resolution and ink rheology are key factors. Screens with larger mesh openings reduce pattern resolution but allow more ink to pass through, which benefits conductivity, but at the cost of feature definition. Conversely, finer meshes improve printed resolution but reduce ink deposition, lowering conductivity, a trade-off illustrated in Fig. 3j. Ink viscosity also plays a critical role. higher viscosity helps suppress post-printing spreading and improves pattern fidelity (Hong et al., J. Mater. Sci. Technol., 67, 145-155 (2021)), yet it also limits ink passage and conductivity. Optimizing print resolution thus requires balancing these competing parameters.
(ii) Ink overflow under extreme shrinkage. When the silicone substrate is shrunk severely, the resulting compressive stress can cause EMP ink to overflow beyond the intended pattern boundaries, distorting the printed features. In this study, the Ecoflex film can sustain large uniaxial strains up to 700%, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 10. Under omnidirectional stretching, a 200-μm-thick film can reach approximately 300% strain, corresponding to an area expansion of ~16×, as demonstrated in the newly added Supplementary Video 1. Theoretically, this allows up to ~94% areal shrinkage, but in practice we observe reliable shrinking only up to ~80%. Beyond this point, EMPs overflow becomes pronounced, leading to line broadening, loss of resolution, and in capacitor structures (e.g., interdigitated electrodes), catastrophic short-circuiting. This overflow persists even with a finer 300-mesh screen. However, when using a finer 420-mesh screen, the ink can no longer pass through to form continuous conductive pathways, presenting a key barrier to achieving features below 50 μm.
Accordingly, we have included the data from our initial orthogonal experiments in Table S1 to show how different screen parameters affect the printing resolution before and after shrinkage. A schematic illustration is provided in Supplementary Fig. 14, and SEM images of EMP overflow under shrinkage are presented in Supplementary Fig. 15, in the supplementary information. ## Paper

## Abstract

Fiber represents a transformative architecture for next-generation wearable electronics, owing to its intrinsic flexibility, spatial compactness, and manufacturing adaptability. However, the geometric incompatibility between curved fiber substrates and conventional planar photolithography/printing techniques has hindered the fabrication of high-density microcircuits on fibers. Here, we introduce a shrinkage-transfer-assisted printing (STAP) strategy that bridges 2D planar circuit fabrication and 1D fiber device construction by shrinking fluidic eutectic gallium-indium (EGaIn) circuits and transferring them onto curved fiber surfaces. This approach achieves a shrinkage ratio of up to 80% with a resolution of 60 μm via scalable screen printing, and employs a capillary-driven transfer process to realize 360° conformal coverage of circuits on fibers. The resulting fiber devices exhibit mechanical robustness over 16,000 bending cycles. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate an electroluminescent fiber display system with individually addressable pixels. This work provides a versatile strategy for manufacturing microcircuits on curved fiber surfaces, opening a route toward scalable and multifunctional fiber electronics.

---

## Introduction

One-dimensional fiber-based architectures are emerging as promising platforms for next-generation flexible electronics, offering substantial potential for miniaturization, integration, and wearability1–5. The inherent structural features of fibers endow them with exceptional mechanical flexibility and processability, enabling versatile design possibilities6. Individual fiber devices can serve as self-sufficient electronic systems while also being directly assembled into advanced architectures, providing considerable design freedom for miniaturized wearable applications7. These unique attributes have driven notable progress in fiber-based technologies for health monitoring8–10, flexible displays11–13, and energy storage/conversion systems14–16.

The pursuit of unprecedented functionality in fiber devices necessitates compatibility between the geometric characteristics and those of functional materials and processing methods17,18. Current strategies to accommodate the high-aspect-ratio 1D geometry of fibers include axial deposition of functional coatings19,20 or incorporation of materials during spinning processes21. Taking advantage of the structural adaptability of fibers, established textile techniques such as twisting, stitching, and weaving further facilitate device integration18,22. Notably, 2D planar substrates support sophisticated electronic functionalities via complex circuitry and integrated components (e.g., printed circuit boards), inspiring a promising approach for fiber devices: direct circuit fabrication on curved fiber surfaces. Such an approach could enhance structural compactness, functional integration, and application versatility in fiber electronics.

However, conventional methods for fabricating electronic components, such as photolithography and direct ink writing, on 2D planes are not directly transferable to fibers, owing to geometric incompatibility with curved surfaces and challenges in achieving sufficient circuit resolution23–25. These limitations motivate an alternative strategy: first constructing electronic components on a 2D platform, then transforming them geometrically for integration onto 1D fibers. Such methodology could combine the advantages of planar fabrication technologies with the intrinsic benefits of fiber geometries, ultimately facilitating the development of high-performance fiber devices.

---

## Results

The STAP process consists of two sequential steps: controlled shrinkage and conformal transfer. First, a silicone substrate (Ecoflex film) is omnidirectional pre-strained to a defined ratio and secured on an acrylic frame to maintain tension (Supplementary Fig. 1, Movie 1). EGaIn circuits are then screen-printed onto the stretched silicone substrate. Upon releasing the tension, the substrate contracts, resulting in a uniform reduction in the circuit size and forming microcircuits (Fig. 1a). Subsequently, the microcircuits are transferred conformally onto the target fiber using a water-soluble PVA carrier film. After dissolving the PVA layer, the EGaIn microcircuits remain intact and adherent to the fiber surface (Supplementary Movie 2). To demonstrate functional applicability, we spray-coated an EL layer consisting of ZnS:Cu particles dispersed in a styrene-ethylene-butylene-styrene (SEBS) matrix onto the fiber, achieving a light-emitting array with individually addressable pixels (Fig. 1b).

The shrinkage ratio of EGaIn microcircuits can be precisely controlled (Supplementary Fig. 2), enabling up to an 80% reduction in circuit area relative to the original printed design while preserving structural integrity and pattern fidelity (Fig. 1c). These microcircuits can be fabricated at arbitrary position along meter-length continuous fiber (Fig. 1d) and achieve 360° full circumferential coverage, thereby maximizing the available surface area for functional device integration (Fig. 1e). The transfer process preserves the microcircuit patterns without noticeable distortion. Owing to the ultrathin nature of the PVA carrier film (20 μm), residual PVA on the fiber surface is negligible and does not compromise the overall flexibility of the system.

The EL functionality of the pixels is driven by the high electric field generated within the microcircuits under pulsed voltage excitation. When an alternating electric field exceeding 2 kV/mm is applied across the luminescent layer coated on the circuits, electrons in ZnS:Cu absorb energy, being promoted to excited states, and emit photons upon returning to their ground states26. Controllable light emission is achieved by optimizing the interelectrode spacing within the microcircuits to maintain an electric field sufficient for luminescence while avoiding dielectric breakdown (Fig. 1f). The STAP strategy improves processing resolution through controlled size reduction, while the circuit fabrication itself remains a macroscale process. This approach readily produces electrode gaps as narrow as 35 μm (Supplementary Fig. 3), exceeding the typical resolution limit of conventional screen-printing methods (50 μm), which is constrained by the mesh size.

Screen-printable conductive ink is crucial for fabricating EGaIn microcircuits. We developed a water-based EGaIn/sericin ink composed of EGaIn with a melting point of 16 °C as the conductive component and silk sericin as the stabilizer (Fig. 2a). Bulk EGaIn was dispersed into EGaIn microparticles (EMPs) by blending it at 20,000 rpm. The resulting EMPs were slightly oxidized in water, forming a surface oxide layer that improves their affinity with sericin. Sericin contains amino acids such as serine, tyrosine, and aspartic acid, which have oxygen-rich functional side groups, as well as cysteine with sulfur-containing side groups27. Consequently, sericin can stably adhere to the surface of EMPs through hydrogen bonding and coordination interactions. This adsorption creates a physical barrier between individual EMPs. Furthermore, sericin is negatively charged in neutral aqueous solution (isoelectric point = 4)28, inducing electrostatic repulsion among sericin-coated EMPs due to Coulombic forces (Fig. 2b). The combined steric and electrostatic stabilization effects allow the EMPs to remain well-dispersed in water for more than one week without agglomeration (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 5).

Microscopic and spectroscopic characterizations confirm the interactions between EMPs and sericin. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) coupled with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) reveals a homogeneous distribution of O, N, and S elements across the EMP surfaces, confirming the presence of sericin adhesion (Fig. 2d). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images directly show a continuous shell layer of sericin coating the EMPs (Fig. 2e). Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) exhibits a red shift of 12.5 cm−1 in the characteristic sericin absorption peak at 3267.3 cm−1 after adsorption onto EMPs (Fig. 2f), suggesting hydrogen bonding formation between sericin and the surface oxide layer29,30. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) further reveals the interactions between sulfur atoms in cysteine residues and the EMP surface. The S 2p spectrum exhibit two characteristic peaks at 167.3 eV and 168.4 eV (Fig. 2g), corresponding to free thiol groups in cysteine31. Upon binding with EMPs, these peaks shift to lower binding energies (160.6 eV and 163.0 eV), consistent with the formation of metal-sulfur bonds or coordination32,33. The peak at 158.8 eV is attributed to the overlap of Ga 3s34. This distinct shift of S 2p peaks provides strong evidence of chemical interactions. Complementary N 1s spectra (Supplementary Fig. 4) reflect changes in nitrogen coordination environments, offering additional support for the sericin-mediated stabilization mechanism.

The affinity between EMPs and sericin endow the EGaIn/sericin ink with high colloidal stability and excellent printability. The size of EMPs can be tuned by varying the blending duration, yielding particles with an averaged diameter of approximately 3 μm that is suitable for unobstructed passage through screen meshes (Fig. 2h, Supplementary Fig. 6). Zeta potential measurements reveal a more negative surface charge for the EGaIn/sericin composite (−12.4 mV) compared to pure sericin solution (−7.4 mV) (Fig. 2i), suggesting that EMPs promote ionization of acidic functional groups in sericin, thereby enhancing electrostatic stabilization. Rheological analyses show that the incorporation of EMPs increases the viscosity of the sericin matrix, consistent with strong interfacial interactions. Notably, the EGaIn/sericin system exhibits a pronounced shear-thinning behavior (Fig. 2j), which is an essential requirement for high-resolution screen printing, as it facilitates flow during printing while ensuring shape retention thereafter35.

The printed circuit patterns are initially non-conductive due to the presence of surface oxides and surrounding polymer barriers, which typically require additional sintering steps, such as mechanical compression or chemical treatment, to form conductive pathways in conventional EGaIn circuits36. Remarkably, the STAP strategy integrates two in situ sintering mechanisms without requiring external interventions. The first mechanism, shrinkage-induced sintering, occurs autonomously during substrate contraction. Prior to screen printing, a pre-stretched silicone substrate is partially treated with air plasma (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Figs. 7, 8) to enhance ink adhesion. A plasma treatment duration of 3 min enables robust attachment of the printed circuit patterns (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Movie 3). Subsequent release of the pre-strain triggers spontaneous conductivity development (Fig. 3c). In samples with pre-stretch ratios of 450%, 300%, and 150%, the resistance evolution follows a characteristic three-stage profile: starting from infinity, dropping rapidly to a finite value, and finally stabilizing (Fig. 3e). All groups reached a resistance of 102 Ω after an initial 50% strain release, exhibiting diminishing returns with further release. Higher pre-strain ratios resulted in lower final resistances (Fig. 3f), indicating more efficient sintering of the EMPs. Mechanistic analysis suggests that the shrinkage of the substrate reduces the interparticle spacing until the friction force (Ff) between EMPs and the substrate exceeds the mechanical strength of the particle shells (Fig. 3d), resulting in shell rupture and EGaIn fusion. Larger pre-stretch amplifies this compressive force, thereby enhancing electrical conductivity. Notably, this sintering process preserves pattern integrity despite internal particle rearrangement.

The transfer-sintering mechanism is activated during the transfer of shrunken EGaIn microcircuits from the silicone substrates to PVA films. As the PVA is peeled from the silicone, continuous metallic patterns become visible on the PVA surface (Fig. 3g), confirming the formation of a conductive pathway. In situ SEM characterization reveals that EGaIn adheres to both surfaces without detectable EMP residues (Fig. 3h), indicating complete sintering. This transfer-induced sintering arises from competitive interfacial adhesion: the plasma-activated silicone and the PVA film both exhibit strong affinity to the EMPs, showing adhesion forces of 0.53 μN and 0.79 μN, respectively (Supplementary Figs. 11, 12). Consequently, the separation process ruptures the oxide shells, triggering instantaneous liquid metal coalescence. The stronger affinity between PVA and EMPs results in preferential transfer of the EGaIn circuits to the PVA surface. The affinity of PVA is primarily attributed to hydrogen bonds between the hydroxyl groups of PVA and the EMPs. To verify the role of hydroxyl groups, comparative adhesion tests were conducted using polyvinyl butyral (PVB), a polymer structurally analogous to PVA but with a portion of its hydroxyl groups blocked by acetal formation. Mechanical measurements reveal that the adhesion force of PVB films toward EMPs is 0.46 μN, significantly lower than that of PVA (0.79 μN) (Supplementary Fig. 12e, f). Laser confocal microscopy further reveals the morphological evolution and gap narrowing during dual-stage sintering, confirming that the STAP strategy synergistically combines circuit miniaturization and conductivity restoration without compromising structural integrity (Fig. 3i, Supplementary Fig. 13). Furthermore, the reduced feature sizes in EGaIn microcircuits directly enhance device integration density, an outcome governed by two principal parameters: the original screen mesh specifications and the applied shrinkage ratio.

The ultimate resolution achievable by STAP is governed by the initial screen-printing precision and the shrinkage behavior of the EMPs on the silicone platform. The intrinsic resolution (Ff) is defined by the screen-printing process determines the fineness of the microcircuit patterns. Screens with higher mesh counts provide finer patterning but reduce ink passage, lowering the amount of deposited EGaIn and creating a fundamental compromise between resolution and conductivity. In this work, 300-mesh represents a practical upper limit. Finer meshes fail to transfer sufficient ink to form continuous pathways even after shrinkage. As shown in Fig. 3j, the x-axis represents the pre-stretch ratio, which correlates with the magnitude of Ff that drives sintering. The y-axis denotes the EMP surface coverage, where lower values impede electrical percolation. The phase boundary identifies the combinations of pre-stretch and coverage that maintain conductivity above the percolation threshold. Moving along this boundary toward higher Ff enables smaller feature sizes while preserving electrical continuity (see Table S2 for electrical conductivity for each point). The resolution and lateral deviation of microcircuits fabricated with different screen meshes were systematically examined under an extreme area shrinkage of 80% (Table S1). This parametric framework study addresses the multi-parameter optimization challenge and facilitates the fabrication of high-resolution microcircuits (Fig. 3k). During shrinking, the compressive stress originating from the recovery of the silicone is transmitted upward through the microcircuit (Supplementary Fig. 14). Under extreme shrinkage, this stress can induce overflow of EMPs beyond the designed pattern boundaries. Since further improvement in the as-printed resolution is hindered by insufficient ink transfer through higher-mesh screens, these two factors together limit the final attainable result resolution (Supplementary Fig. 15).

The capillary-driven transfer process enables precise conformal wrapping of EGaIn microcircuit onto fiber substrates. Aramid fiber is chosen as the substrate due to its intrinsic hydrophilicity and relatively high dielectric constant. When a water droplet is introduced at the interface between the PVA film and the fiber, capillary forces induce radial liquid propagation along both the axial and circumferential directions of the fiber, simultaneously dissolving the PVA matrix and promoting interfacial adhesion (Fig. 4a). This process is governed by the thermodynamics of wetting, as described by the following equation (w = water, F = fiber, P = PVA):

ΔG T,p = γ w,P + γ w,F − γ Air,P − γ Air,F (1)

Spontaneous wrapping occurs when ΔG T,p < 0. Given the hydrophilic nature of both PVA and aramid fibers (contact angles < 90°), the following relationships hold:

cosθ w,P = (γ Air,P − γ w,P) / γ w,Air > 0 (2)

cosθ w,F = (γ Air,F − γ w,F) / γ w,Air > 0 (3)

Substituting (2) and (3) into Eq. (1) confirms ΔG T,p < 0, validating the self-driven nature of the transfer mechanism. This ensures conformal contact and reliable adhesion of the microcircuit to the fiber surface without external energy input.

Consequently, water droplets undergo spontaneous downward propagation through the capillary channels formed between the fiber and PVA film. Hydration-induced plasticization softens the PVA, reducing its modulus from 5 GPa to a compliant, rubbery state that enables conformal wrapping around the fiber circumference. Meanwhile, the decreased interfacial tension γ w,P further promotes wetting and adhesion (Fig. 4b). This transfer process demonstrates broad applicability across varying degrees of dimensional reduction (2D→1D). EGaIn microcircuits with shrinkage ratios ranging from 50% to 80% retain structural integrity and pattern fidelity after transfer (Fig. 4c), enabling on-demand fabrication of fiber devices with tunable feature sizes down to 60 μm (Fig. 4d).

Preserving pattern fidelity during fiber device integration is critical, where any circuit discontinuities or short circuits would lead to device failure. Radial gap analysis reveals a dimensional variation of ≤5% across the full 360° circumference (Fig. 4e), confirming the non-destructive nature of our transfer process. Notably, this transfer step can also be applied to fibers of different materials and diameters (Supplementary Fig. 19), and can be repeated on one fiber to construct a multilayer circuit (Supplementary Fig. 20).

The resulting fiber devices exhibit exceptional mechanical compliance, enduring 16,000 bending cycles at a curvature radius of 1.6 cm with only a 1.4% increase in resistance. The fiber microcircuit can be bent to a critical radius (rc, defined as the bending radius at which ΔR/R₀ begins to exceed 200%) of 2.3 mm (Fig. 4f), demonstrating good robustness for wearable applications. This performance originates from the intrinsic fluidity and strain-insensitive conductivity of EGaIn, as confirmed by microscopy observations of continuous EGaIn pathways during bending (Supplementary Fig. 21). The bending limit of the fiber microcircuit is governed by the PVA adhesive layer, whose flexibility increases with temperature and humidity, leading to different critical radii across different environmental conditions (Supplementary Fig. 22). The shrinkage ratio of EGaIn microcircuits, modulated via the STAP process, directly governs the performance of fiber devices. Capacitance measurements of interdigitated electrodes reveal a 103 enhancement (10 Hz) as the shrinkage ratio increases from 50% to 80% (Fig. 4g), attributed to a reduced interelectrode spacing and increased effective electrode area.

The EL performance of the pixels is determined by electric field intensity (E), which we optimized through precise control of the shrinkage ratio. Finite element simulations of the electric field distribution (Fig. 4h) identified 2 kV/mm as the minimum field required to activate ZnS:Cu particles. Excessively large gaps (>50 μm) result in a reduced number of activated phosphor particles due to field decay, whereas undersized gaps (<25 μm) lead to highly concentrated fields that induce dielectric breakdown. Although the aramid fiber substrate has high tolerance to strong electric fields37, the breakdown of the emissive functional layer remains affecting luminescence efficiency. Thus, an intermediate gap width is required to achieve optimal luminescence. Experimentally, peak luminance is achieved at gap distances of 50–60 μm, where the simulated electric field maximizes the excitation area within the phosphor layer while avoiding dielectric failure (Fig. 4i).

Guided by these design principles, we successfully fabricated an EL pixel array on a fiber. The intrinsic flexibility of the fiber, the EGaIn circuitry, and the SEBS matrix works synergistically to sustain device functionality under mechanical deformation, as demonstrated by a fully operational curved array (Fig. 4j). The pixel array is designed with (2n-3) contact points to individually address n EL pixels, maximizing the number of controllable elements within a limited area (5 contacts controlling 7 pixels in Fig. 4k). Functionalization was carried out by spray-coating a ZnS:Cu/SEBS dispersion, followed by ambient drying to form the electroluminescence layer. Selective pixel activation can be achieved by electrical addressing through designated contacts (Fig. 4l, Supplementary Movie 4), enabling the multiplexed display on a single fiber. Luminance stability remains 94% when bent to a radius of 15 mm, but then decreases rapidly as the curvature increases further (Supplementary Fig. 23). Single-fiber displays, featuring pixel-level addressability, can be seamlessly woven into protective garments for dynamic visual communication. In critical scenarios such as firefighting, rescue operations, and outdoor exploration, they can provide real-time navigation, hazard alerts, or team status. They also enable monitoring of vital signs for medical assistance and facilitate communication by displaying information for individuals with speech or language barriers. It is noted that the STAP process is also compatible with other typical commercially available inks besides the EGaIn/sericin ink (Supplementary Fig. 24). This STAP strategy overcomes the long-standing challenge of integrating high-precision microcircuits onto curved fiber substrates, paving the way for multifunctional and high-density wearable electronics. Further efforts on developing automated stretching and continuous transfer systems could improve the scalability of STAP and facilitate its adoption in practical manufacturing settings.

## Methods

Materials
All materials were used as received. EGaIn (75%Ga, 25%In, melting point 16 °C) was purchased from Alibaba. Silk sericin and PVA (MW: 100,000) were purchased from Macklin. ZnS:Cu phosphor powder was purchased from Shanghai Keyan Phosphor Technology Co., Ltd. Ecoflex 0030 was purchased from Smooth-On. Aramid fiber was purchased from DuPont. SEBS and chloroform were purchased from Sigma. Ag/AgCl ink and PEDOT:PSS ink were purchased from Prtronic, and the carbon ink was obtained from Loctite. All inks were used as received, without further purification or modification.

Fabrication of EGaIn/sericin ink
First, prepare 100 ml of 2 wt% sericin aqueous solution. Using a syringe, inject 4 ml of EGaIn into the solution, and disperse it using an IKA mill at a speed of 20,000 rpm for 1 min. Subsequently, cool the mixture to 20 °C using an ice-water bath, and repeat the process three times.

Fabrication of Shrunk microcircuits
The fabrication of shrunk microcircuits was carried out in two main steps: screen printing and pattern shrinkage. First, a 200 μm-thick Ecoflex film was omnidirectionally stretched and mounted onto a clean acrylic frame under tension. Next, a patterned screen was placed on the surface of the Ecoflex film as a mask, and the sample was exposed to air plasma for 3 min. Then, EGaIn/sericin ink was screen-printed onto the film. After drying, the EGaIn circuit was formed on the silicone substrate. Pattern shrinkage was achieved by releasing the pre-strained Ecoflex film from the acrylic frame, resulting in the contraction of the substrate and the formation of the final shrunk microcircuits. All the processes, including the fabrication of shrunk microcircuits and their transfer, were performed at 20 °C and 50% relative humidity, unless otherwise specified.

Process of transferring microcircuits
The transfer of the microcircuit was accomplished using a PVA carrier film. A 20 μm thick PVA film was prepared by casting, then handled with tweezers, and its bottom surface was briefly contacted with a water surface for 0.5 s to achieve partial hydration. The moistened film was then carefully laminated onto the Ecoflex substrate bearing the microcircuit. After allowing the PVA film to partially dissolve, the assembly was dried under 60 °C for 30 min to enhance adhesion and facilitate the formation of a continuous bilayer. Finally, the PVA film was peeled off, transferring the highly conductive, intact EGaIn microcircuit to the PVA surface.

Fabrication of single-point controllable EL fiber device
The fabricated PVA film carrying the microcircuit was placed onto the target fiber surface. Using a syringe, water was carefully applied along the edges of the PVA film to allow capillary action to penetrate the interface, enabling the circuit to adhere to the fiber surface and forming the fiber circuit. Special care should be taken to ensure that the water is applied to the gaps between the PVA film and the fiber, rather than directly on the surface of the PVA film. Upon complete dissolution of the PVA, the circuit remained attached to the fiber, forming a continuous fiber-integrated microcircuit. The assembly was then dried at 60 °C for 30 min to enhance stability. Subsequently, an electroluminescent layer was applied by spray-coating a formulated ink suspension consisting of ZnS:Cu fluorescent powder, SEBS elastomer, and chloroform (mass ratio: 1 g: 0.5 g: 5 g). The coated fiber was dried again to evaporate the solvent, forming a solid emissive composite layer. Finally, the device was completed by connecting the fiber circuit to an external power supply for activation and operation.

Morphology characterization
Transmission electron microscopy (JEOL, JEM-2100F) and scanning electron microscopy (Thermo Fisher, Phenom XL G2 Desktop SEM) were used to characterize the morphology of EGaIn microparticles and microcircuits. The in situ observation of PVA/Ecoflex delamination and the shrinkage-sintering of microcircuits was carried out using an SEM equipped with an in situ tensile holder. Image processing and EGaIn microparticle diameter analysis were conducted using ImageJ software. Laser confocal microscopy (Zeiss, LSM900) was used to observe surface morphology changes during the shrinking and transfer processes of the microcircuits.

Spectroscopic and rheological characterization
Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, BRUKER, VERTEX) was used to evaluate hydrogen bonding interactions between EGaIn and sericin. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Fisher, ESCALAB Xi+) was used to analyze the coordination interactions between EGaIn and sericin. Viscosity measurements were conducted using a rotational rheometer (Anton Paar, MCR302).

Electrical and mechanical characterization
Electrical characterization was performed using an electrochemical workstation (Shanghai Chenhua, CHI760E). Mechanical tests were conducted using a SHIMADZU AGS-X universal testing machine. For simultaneous electromechanical characterization, the fiber device was mounted onto the tensile tester while electrically connected to the workstation via wires. Data acquisition from both instruments was synchronized through time alignment to correlate mechanical strain with electrical response. Repeated bending deformation was performed at a maximum curvature radius of 16 mm, at 20 °C and relative humidity of 50%, with a frequency of 1 Hz. The samples were stored in a temperature- and humidity-controlled chamber for 3 h before the test.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents a highly original approach to addressing the persistent challenge of integrating microscale circuits onto curved fiber surfaces. The proposed shrinkage-transfer-assisted printing (STAP) method elegantly bridges the gap between 2D circuit fabrication and 1D fiber device realization, achieving impressive miniaturization (up to 80% shrinkage) and 360° conformal coverage. The concept is novel, technically sound, and well supported by systematic experiments. The combination of stress-engineered silicone substrates, EGaIn/sericin ink chemistry, and capillary-driven transfer represents a meaningful advance in fiber-based electronics.
The manuscript is generally well written, visually clear, and methodologically detailed. It convincingly demonstrates functionality through the electroluminescent fiber device. The work is clearly distinct from previously published studies—including our earlier Nature Communications paper on integrated microfibre electronics—by offering a different dimensional transformation and processing strategy.
That said, a few aspects need clarification and strengthening before acceptance. These concern (1) the universality and scalability of the claimed “universal fabrication strategy,” (2) quantitative treatment of the scaling-down limit for metallic patterns, and (3) mechanical durability and interfacial reliability under extended cyclic deformation.
Overall, this is an excellent and innovative contribution that will attract broad attention in the field of fiber electronics and soft-matter circuit integration. The concept of geometric transformation from 2D to 1D is elegant, and the results are compelling.
Addressing the issues above, particularly regarding the scaling limit and mechanical reliability, will further strengthen the manuscript’s impact and technical completeness.
Major Comments
- The Introduction concludes that STAP is a “universal fabrication strategy,” yet experimental demonstrations are limited to EGaIn and PVA-based transfer. To substantiate this claim, the authors should briefly discuss whether the STAP process is compatible with other inks (e.g., silver nanoparticle, conductive polymer) or elastomeric substrates.
- A comparative comment on scalability with respect to textile-level or roll-to-roll fabrication methods would provide valuable context for its practical universality.
- What is possible resolution and Scaling-Down Limitations?

- Providing a scaling analysis or discussing the potential challenges in pushing esolution below 50 μm would be insightful. For instance, could oxide shell rupture or uneven compressive stress during shrinkage impose a lower limit?

However, the detailed stress conditions (bending radius, strain amplitude, test frequency) should be more explicitly stated in Methods or figure captions to allow fair comparison with prior works.
- Since the circuit–fiber interface is critical, it would be helpful to discuss or test failure modes such as delamination or crack initiation, particularly under humidity or temperature variation. Supplementary Fig. 14 shows morphological stability but does not provide long-term cycling data.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript is generally well written and clearly presented. However, there are several issues that limit the overall scope and relevence of the work.
Material specificity:
The materials used in the study are very specialized and are not easily replaced or adapted to other functional materials (substrate, ink, GaIn ....)
Scalability and reproducibility:
Key steps in the process—such as pre-stretching, tension release, transferring onto a PVA sheet, water-assisted transfer, and the shrinkage of the printed circuits—introduce a lot of variability and are not easily scalable. As a result, achieving consistent reproducibility is challenging. In addition, the conductivity variations that come from shrinkage sintering and transfer sintering need to be supported with more detailed statistical data.
Multilayer printing limitations:
The approach does not seem capable of true multilayer printing. In the demonstrated device, the conductive layer is printed and transferred onto the thread, while the luminescent layer is applied by coating rather than printing. This highlights an inherent limitation of the technique.
Limited use on small-diameter substrates:
The method is demonstrated only on threads a few millimeters in diameter. Its potential for use on finer fibers or true one-dimensional substrates is not addressed, which restricts the broader relevance of the work.

We appreciate the insightful questions regarding resolution and scaling-down limitations. Since Comments #3-5 are closely related, we address them collectively below. We have supplemented the discussion with schematic illustrations, SEM characterizations and additional data. The fundamental limits on resolution and miniaturization arise from two main aspects:
(i) Printing resolution on the pre-stretched silicone substrate. The initial patterning fidelity is governed by the screen-printing process. The resolution here refers to the clarity and continuity of the printed EGaIn/sericin pattern after the ink passes through the screen mesh. This printed pattern must be optically distinguishable and electrically continuous after shrinkage. Screen mesh resolution and ink rheology are key factors. Screens with larger mesh openings reduce pattern resolution but allow more ink to pass through, which benefits conductivity, but at the cost of feature definition. Conversely, finer meshes improve printed resolution but reduce ink deposition, lowering conductivity, a trade-off illustrated in Fig. 3j. Ink viscosity also plays a critical role. higher viscosity helps suppress post-printing spreading and improves pattern fidelity (Hong et al., J. Mater. Sci. Technol., 67, 145-155 (2021)), yet it also limits ink passage and conductivity. Optimizing print resolution thus requires balancing these competing parameters.
(ii) Ink overflow under extreme shrinkage. When the silicone substrate is shrunk severely, the resulting compressive stress can cause EMP ink to overflow beyond the intended pattern boundaries, distorting the printed features. In this study, the Ecoflex film can sustain large uniaxial strains up to 700%, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 10. Under omnidirectional stretching, a 200-μm-thick film can reach approximately 300% strain, corresponding to an area expansion of ~16×, as demonstrated in the newly added Supplementary Video 1. Theoretically, this allows up to ~94% areal shrinkage, but in practice we observe reliable shrinking only up to ~80%. Beyond this point, EMPs overflow becomes pronounced, leading to line broadening, loss of resolution, and in capacitor structures (e.g., interdigitated electrodes), catastrophic short-circuiting. This overflow persists even with a finer 300-mesh screen. However, when using a finer 420-mesh screen, the ink can no longer pass through to form continuous conductive pathways, presenting a key barrier to achieving features below 50 μm.
Accordingly, we have included the data from our initial orthogonal experiments in Table S1 to show how different screen parameters affect the printing resolution before and after shrinkage. Comment #2:
Scalability and reproducibility:
Key steps in the process—such as pre-stretching, tension release, transferring onto a PVA sheet, water-assisted transfer, and the shrinkage of the printed circuits—introduce a lot of variability and are not easily scalable. As a result, achieving consistent reproducibility is challenging. Reply:
Thank you for your insightful comment. We agree that the STAP workflow involves multiple steps, imposing challenges for scalability and reproducibility.
Regarding reproducibility, all the key steps, including pre-stretching, tension regulation, circuit shrinkage, hydration of the PVA film, and the final transfer, can be governed by controllable experimental parameters. The pre-stretching process is performed on a stress-engineered silicone platform with adjustable pre-strain, and the deformation state can be monitored using an orthogonal finite-element grid (Supplementary Video 1). We also investigated the effects of shrinkage and transfer parameters on the restoration of EMP conductivity. The PVA-assisted transfer reliably recovers the conductivity of EMP networks to the same order of magnitude as bulk EGaIn, and experimental results show that the transfer and reconstruction process proceeds with a very high success rate (nearly 100% for across 20 times trials). Besides, the screen printing in the STAP process is an industrial-scale patterning method widely used in textile manufacturing.
Regarding scalability, we acknowledge that our current laboratory-scale preparation has limitations. Despite of this, we think it has potential for large-scale applications as the mechanism itself does not impose fundamental barriers to scaling. The stress-engineered 2D silicone platform could be scaled up by using larger substrates. However, continuous large-scale manufacturing would require an automated stretching system capable of applying uniform tension along the entire film. After shrinkage, the silicone film carrying the microcircuits could be brought into contact with a continuous PVA roll, following by wetting, drying, transfer and collection along a production line. This approach appears feasible and would mainly require engineering design for automate wetting and rapid drying. Your comment provides a forward-looking perspective on the practical deployment of STAP.

Multilayer printing limitations:
The approach does not seem capable of true multilayer printing. In the demonstrated device, the conductive layer is printed and transferred onto the thread, while the luminescent layer is applied by coating rather than printing. This highlights an inherent limitation of the technique.
Reply:
Thank you for your insightful comment. Accordingly, we carried out further experiment to explore the possibility for construction multilayer circuits with the STAP strategy. We found that multilayer circuits can be constructed on separate PVA films using different screen-printing masks. These films can then be sequentially transferred to the aligned position of the fiber surface. We also considered that possibility for the printing of the luminescent layer. However, as for the STAP process involves the wetting and drying of the PVA film, constructing a non-permeable luminescent layer on the film would influence the wetting behavior, and thus introduce non-uniform stress.

Comment #4:
Limited use on small-diameter substrates:
The method is demonstrated only on threads a few millimeters in diameter. Its potential for use on finer fibers or true one-dimensional substrates is not addressed, which restricts the broader relevance of the work
Reply:
Thank you for your raising this critical comment the use of smaller-diameter fibers. We agree that extending the method to finer one-dimensional substrates is an important direction for broader applicability.
In the present work, the fiber devices were designed primarily to demonstrate single-pixel electroluminescence. As fiber diameter decreases, pixel crosstalk between densely packed microcircuits becomes significantly more pronounced. To ensure clear functionality and avoid signal interference, we therefore used relatively thicker fibers in the main demonstrations.
In this work, the minimum diameter of fibers we used is 1.5 mm. We think the minimum usable fiber diameter in our approach is constrained mainly by two factors: (1) the achievable printing resolution, and (2) the shrinkage limit of the substrate. Together, these define the smallest reliable circuit feature size, which in then determines how thin a fiber can be reliably patterned. Moving to significantly thinner fibers will require further downscaling of the circuit dimensions, which is one of the goals of our future work.
Accordingly, we have added discussion on the key challenges in the main text, and images of fiber devices fabricated on 2.0 mm and 1.5 mm fibers made of different materials (Supplementary Fig. 19) and multilayer circuits fabricated on 1.5 mm fibers (Supplementary Fig. 20) in the supplementary information.
